label: Tractable classes of SAT
lesson:
# Tractable classes of SAT

SAT is NP-complete, but several syntactic classes are solvable in polynomial time, and a surprising share of the constraints that EDA tools generate fall into them. Recognizing a tractable fragment lets a tool skip the general solver or hand it a much easier problem. Schaefer's dichotomy theorem says that for Boolean constraint languages this is all there is: each language is either in one of a few polynomial classes or NP-complete. Knowing where the line falls tells a designer when a special-purpose algorithm exists.

## 2-SAT and the implication graph

A CNF in which every clause has at most two literals is solved in linear time. Each clause $(p \lor q)$ is equivalent to the implications $\neg p \to q$ and $\neg q \to p$; draw them as edges on $2n$ literal vertices. The formula is unsatisfiable exactly when some variable $x$ and $\neg x$ lie in the same strongly connected component, since then $x$ implies $\neg x$ and $\neg x$ implies $x$.

The clause $(a \lor \neg b)$ gives the edges $\neg a \to \neg b$ and $b \to a$, so a 2-CNF with $m$ clauses has $2m$ edges. Finding components with Tarjan's algorithm and reading off an assignment in reverse topological order takes $O(n + m)$. Binary clauses are common in practice, from equivalences and implications, and modern solvers store them in a separate implication structure for speed.

## Horn clauses and forward chaining

A Horn clause has at most one positive literal, such as $(\neg a \lor \neg b \lor c)$, which reads as the rule $a \wedge b \to c$. Horn-SAT is solved by starting with every variable false and setting a variable true only when some clause forces it. If a clause with no positive literal ends up with all its variables true, the formula is unsatisfiable; otherwise the forced set is a model.

That model is the least one in the componentwise order, because Horn models are closed under intersection. With linear-time bookkeeping (Dowling and Gallier), unit propagation alone decides Horn formulas, which is why Horn fragments are solved with no search at all. Dual-Horn, at most one negative literal, is symmetric.

## XOR constraints and where hardness begins

Constraints of the form $x_1 \oplus x_2 \oplus \dots \oplus x_k = c$ are linear equations over GF(2) and are solved by Gaussian elimination in polynomial time. In CNF without auxiliary variables a single such XOR needs $2^{k-1}$ clauses, and CDCL handles long XOR chains badly, so solvers aimed at cryptographic and arithmetic instances add native Gaussian elimination.

Allowing three literals per OR clause breaks all of these: 3-SAT is NP-complete. Schaefer (1978) showed the tractable Boolean constraint languages are exactly the 0-valid, 1-valid, Horn, dual-Horn, bijunctive (2-CNF) and affine (XOR) ones; everything else is NP-complete. A useful consequence for tool builders: if a problem's constraints are all binary or all Horn, a polynomial algorithm exists and a general SAT call is overkill.

## Going deeper

Dowling and Gallier, "Linear-time algorithms for testing the satisfiability of propositional Horn formulae", Journal of Logic Programming (1984). Schaefer, "The complexity of satisfiability problems", STOC (1978).

label: Algorithm analysis for Boolean tools
lesson:
# Algorithm analysis for Boolean tools

Boolean tools live on the edge between polynomial and exponential cost. A tool designer must predict, before writing code, whether an approach scales: how much memory an explicit representation takes, how many calls a recursion makes, and how a measured runtime will extrapolate to the next design size. These estimates come from three habits: count the size of the data, write the recurrence of the algorithm, and know what each growth rate does when the input grows.

## Memory of an explicit truth table

A truth table of $n$ variables has $2^n$ bits. Packed into $w$-bit words it needs $2^n / w$ words, $2^{n-6}$ for 64-bit words when $n \ge 6$. A 16-input table is 1,024 words (8 KiB), a 20-input table 16,384 words (128 KiB), and a 30-input table $2^{24}$ words, 128 MiB.

Each added variable doubles the memory, which is why truth tables are used for cuts of up to about 16 inputs and why everything larger is represented implicitly by AIGs, BDDs or CNF. When a design flow computes a truth table per node, multiply by the number of nodes too: a million 6-input cuts at one word each is 8 MB, but a million 12-input cuts is 512 MB.

## Recurrences of recursive Boolean algorithms

Recursive algorithms that split on a variable obey recurrences. A tautology check that splits on one variable per level without pruning makes $T(k) = 2T(k-1) + 1$ calls with $T(0) = 1$, which unrolls to $T(k) = 2^{k+1} - 1$: 31 calls for 4 variables, about two million for 20. A procedure that does $c$ units of work and recurses on both cofactors satisfies $T(k) = 2T(k-1) + c$, still $\Theta(2^k)$.

Pruning changes the base, not the shape: if one branch always has one fewer variable and the other two fewer, $T(k) = T(k-1) + T(k-2) + 1$ grows like $1.618^k$. Memoization changes the shape: a recursion that caches results per distinct subfunction does work proportional to the number of distinct subfunctions, which is the BDD size, not $2^k$.

## Extrapolating exponential running time

Measured runtimes extrapolate by growth rate. For $\Theta(2^n)$, adding $k$ variables multiplies time by $2^k$: an exact method taking 2 s at $n = 40$ takes 8 s at $n = 42$ and about 34 minutes at $n = 50$. For $\Theta(n^3)$, scaling $n$ by a factor $r$ multiplies time by $r^3$: doubling the size costs 8 times as long.

The practical test is what happens on the next technology node or the next design generation. Polynomial algorithms degrade gracefully; exponential ones hit a wall. That is why EDA engines that are exponential in the worst case (SAT, exact minimization) are wrapped in resource limits and fall back to heuristics, and why an engine's documentation should state its complexity in the size of the actual input, which for a truth table is already $2^n$.

## Going deeper

Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, "Introduction to Algorithms" (4th ed., 2022), chapters 3 and 4. Knuth, "The Art of Computer Programming", volume 4A, on Boolean function representation costs.

label: Amortized analysis
lesson:
# Amortized analysis

Amortized analysis bounds the total cost of a sequence of operations, even when single operations are occasionally expensive. Boolean engines are full of such structures: unique tables and computed tables in BDD packages that double when full, clause databases that grow and are periodically reduced, the trail of a SAT solver, incremental timing graphs. A designer who knows the amortized cost can promise constant time per operation where a worst-case bound would say linear.

## The binary counter

Incrementing a binary counter flips all trailing 1s to 0 and one 0 to 1. A single increment can flip many bits (0111 to 1000 flips four), but bit $j$ flips only once every $2^j$ increments. Over $N$ increments from 0 the total is $\sum_j \lfloor N / 2^j \rfloor$, which equals $2N - s(N)$, where $s(N)$ is the number of 1s in the binary form of $N$.

For $N = 8$ the flips per increment are 1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1, 4, totaling 15 $= 16 - 1$. So the amortized cost is under 2 flips per increment, although the worst single increment costs $\log_2 N + 1$. The same argument bounds Gray-code enumeration and the cost of incrementally stepping through cofactor assignments.

## Doubling hash tables

A hash table that doubles its capacity when full copies every stored entry into the new array. Starting from capacity 1, the copies happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, ..., up to the largest power of two below $N$, so the total number of copies after $N$ inserts is less than $2N$. With 9 inserts the table grows at sizes 1, 2, 4 and 8, copying $1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15$ entries.

BDD unique tables, AIG structural-hashing tables and SAT watch lists all grow this way. Growing by a constant factor is essential: growing by a fixed amount (say 1,000 slots each time) makes the total copying quadratic in $N$.

## Cost per operation

Add the direct cost and the copying cost, then divide by the number of operations. For the 9 inserts above: 9 units of insertion plus 15 units of copying is 24, or about 2.67 per insert. The potential method gives a clean bound: with $\Phi = 2 \cdot \text{size} - \text{capacity}$, each insert has amortized cost at most 3, because the potential saved by cheap inserts pays for the next doubling.

Amortized bounds are about totals, not latency. A single resize of a unique table holding $10^8$ nodes still stalls the tool, which is why production BDD packages resize incrementally or during garbage collection, and why an interactive or agent-driven loop that needs predictable response times may prefer worst-case structures.

## Going deeper

Tarjan, "Amortized computational complexity", SIAM Journal on Algebraic and Discrete Methods (1985). Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, "Introduction to Algorithms" (4th ed., 2022), chapter 16.

label: Randomized algorithms and random simulation
prereqs: Expectation of a function of a random variable
lesson:
# Randomized algorithms and random simulation

Randomized algorithms use coin flips to be faster or simpler than any known deterministic method, at the price of a bounded probability of error or a random running time. In Boolean reasoning the most important one is random simulation: apply random input vectors to two circuits and compare. It finds most bugs almost for free, but it can only show that circuits differ, never that they are equal. Quantifying what a clean simulation run proves is a computation every equivalence-checking flow depends on.

## The chance that random vectors miss a difference

Suppose $f$ and $g$ differ on $d$ of the $2^n$ input vectors, so a uniform random vector exposes the difference with probability $p = d / 2^n$. With $t$ independent vectors, all of them miss with probability $(1 - p)^t \approx e^{-pt}$.

For $n = 12$, $d = 128$ and $t = 48$: $p = 128 / 4096 = 1/32$, and $(31/32)^{48} \approx 0.218$. One run in five misses the bug. The danger is the small-$d$ case: a corner-case bug on a handful of vectors in a 64-input block has $p$ around $10^{-18}$, and no feasible simulation will find it. This is a one-sided error: a mismatch found is certain, a mismatch not found proves nothing.

## How many vectors are enough

To push the miss probability below $\varepsilon$, solve $(1 - p)^t \le \varepsilon$: $t \ge \ln \varepsilon / \ln(1 - p)$, approximately $\ln(1/\varepsilon) / p$. For $n = 14$, $d = 128$ and $\varepsilon = 0.1$, $p = 1/128$ and $t = \lceil \ln 0.1 / \ln(127/128) \rceil = 294$.

The required count scales as $1/p$, so halving the size of the difference doubles the vectors needed. A simulator can make $p$ larger by biasing vectors toward suspicious regions (as constrained-random verification does), but no fixed budget certifies equivalence. That is why SAT-sweeping engines use simulation only to propose candidate equivalences and then prove them with SAT.

## Expected time to the first counterexample

Draw vectors until one exposes the difference. The number drawn is geometric with success probability $p$, so its expectation is $1/p$. For $n = 10$ and $d = 64$, $p = 1/16$ and the expected number of vectors is 16.

Randomized algorithms come in two kinds. Monte Carlo algorithms have bounded running time and a probability of a wrong answer, like simulation-based equivalence with a fixed budget. Las Vegas algorithms are always right but have random running time, like a SAT solver with random restarts. Schoening's random walk for 3-SAT is a Monte Carlo algorithm that finds a satisfying assignment, if one exists, with high probability in $O((4/3)^n)$ time up to polynomial factors, better than the $2^n$ of brute force.

## Going deeper

Mishchenko, Chatterjee, Jiang and Brayton, "FRAIGs: a unifying representation for logic synthesis and verification", technical report, UC Berkeley (2005).

label: P, NP and coNP
lesson:
# P, NP and coNP

Complexity classes tell a tool designer what kind of algorithm to look for. A problem in P has an algorithm whose time is polynomial in the input size. A problem in NP has short, quickly checkable certificates for its yes answers, and coNP for its no answers. Satisfiability, the question "can this circuit output 1?", is in NP; tautology and combinational equivalence, "do these circuits agree on every input?", are in coNP. Most of verification lives on the coNP side, which is why proofs, not just answers, matter there.

## Decision problems and polynomial time

Complexity theory classifies decision problems, yes or no questions, by running time as a function of input length. Is there an input that sets this output to 1? Does this graph have a vertex cover of size at most $k$? Optimization and counting versions are related but distinct.

The input length matters more than it seems. An algorithm that takes $O(2^n)$ steps on a function given as an explicit truth table of $2^n$ bits is linear in its input, so many truth-table problems are in P. The same question asked of a formula or circuit, whose size can be polynomial in $n$, may be NP-hard. 2-SAT, Horn-SAT and checking equality of two ROBDDs in one shared manager (a pointer comparison) are in P; 3-SAT is not known to be.

## Certificates and NP

A problem is in NP when every yes-instance has a certificate of polynomial length that a polynomial-time verifier accepts, and no no-instance has one. For SAT the certificate is a satisfying assignment, checked by evaluating every clause. For vertex cover it is the set of at most $k$ vertices, checked edge by edge.

Membership in NP is an upper bound: trying every certificate solves the problem in exponential time, and nothing better is implied. P is contained in NP, and whether they are equal is open. SAT is also self-reducible: a decision procedure finds a model with about $n$ further calls, fixing one variable at a time and keeping the value under which the formula stays satisfiable.

## coNP and the shape of verification problems

coNP is the class of problems whose no-instances have short certificates. Tautology is the standard example: a single input vector on which the circuit outputs 0 refutes it. Combinational equivalence is coNP-complete for the same reason, since a distinguishing vector is a short certificate of non-equivalence.

This asymmetry shapes tools. When a SAT solver finds the miter of two circuits satisfiable, the model is a counterexample anyone can check in linear time. When it reports UNSAT, the circuits are equivalent, but no short certificate of that is known in general; if every unsatisfiable formula had a polynomial-size proof checkable in polynomial time, NP would equal coNP. Solvers therefore emit proofs such as DRAT, which can be long but are checked by small independent programs.

## Going deeper

Arora and Barak, "Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach" (2009), chapters 1 and 2. Sipser, "Introduction to the Theory of Computation" (3rd ed., 2012), chapter 7.

label: Polynomial-time reductions
lesson:
# Polynomial-time reductions

A reduction from problem A to problem B is a polynomial-time transformation of every instance of A into an instance of B with the same yes or no answer. Reductions are how complexity transfers: they prove that a new problem is hard, and they are also how tools solve problems, by encoding them into SAT, ILP or graph problems that have good solvers. The two uses run in opposite directions, and confusing them is the most common error in arguments about EDA problem complexity.

## What a reduction must preserve

A many-one (Karp) reduction is a function $r$ computable in polynomial time such that $x \in A$ exactly when $r(x) \in B$. Write $A \le_p B$. It must map yes-instances to yes-instances and no-instances to no-instances; it need not preserve the number of solutions, although parsimonious reductions do, which matters for counting.

Two consequences follow. If $A \le_p B$ and B is in P, then A is in P: run $r$, then B's algorithm, polynomial composed with polynomial. If $A \le_p B$ and A is NP-hard, then B is NP-hard. Reductions compose, which is how chains such as SAT to 3-SAT to independent set to vertex cover are built.

## 3-SAT to independent set

Karp's reduction maps a 3-CNF with $m$ clauses to a graph: one vertex per literal occurrence, a triangle joining the three literals of each clause, and an edge between every pair of complementary literals in different clauses. Ask for an independent set of size $k = m$. An independent set can take at most one vertex per triangle, so size $m$ means one literal per clause, and the complementary edges forbid choosing both $x$ and $\neg x$: such a set exists exactly when the formula is satisfiable.

For $(x_1 \lor x_2 \lor x_3)(\neg x_1 \lor \neg x_2 \lor x_3)$: 6 vertices, 6 triangle edges, and 2 complementary edges ($x_1$ with $\neg x_1$, $x_2$ with $\neg x_2$), so 8 edges and $k = 2$. Picking $x_3$ in both clauses is an independent set of size 2, matching the model $x_3 = 1$.

## Choosing the direction

To show a new problem X is hard, reduce a known hard problem to X: every instance of the hard problem becomes an instance of X. To solve X with existing tools, reduce X to a solved problem, for example encode X as SAT. The second direction gives an algorithm and an upper bound and says nothing about hardness.

So encoding clock-gating legality or test generation into CNF shows those problems are in NP, provided the encoding is polynomial, while Ibarra and Sahni's construction of a circuit whose fault is detectable exactly when a given circuit is satisfiable shows test generation is NP-hard. An argument that reduces X to SAT and concludes "X is NP-hard" has the arrow backwards.

## Going deeper

label: NP-completeness
lesson:
# NP-completeness

A problem is NP-complete when it is in NP and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time. NP-complete problems are the hardest in NP: a polynomial algorithm for any one of them would give one for all, and none is known. Many core EDA problems, from SAT and test generation to graph coloring, partitioning and placement decisions, are NP-complete or NP-hard, and that fact is why EDA engines are built around heuristics, approximations, resource limits and exact solvers that are fast only on typical instances.

## The Cook-Levin theorem

Cook (1971) and Levin independently proved that SAT is NP-complete. The idea: any NP problem has a polynomial-time verifier that reads an instance and a certificate. For a fixed input size, that verifier's computation unrolls into a circuit of polynomial size whose free inputs are the certificate bits. The instance is a yes-instance exactly when some certificate makes the circuit accept, a circuit-satisfiability question.

Circuit-SAT then reduces to CNF-SAT by the Tseitin encoding, which adds one variable per gate and a few clauses per gate, linear in circuit size and satisfiable exactly when the circuit is. The canonical CNF would not do, since it can be exponential. Tseitin's formula is equisatisfiable, not equivalent: its models live over the inputs plus the gate variables.

## Proving a new problem NP-complete

Two steps are required. First, show the problem is in NP by naming a polynomial certificate and verifier. Second, reduce a known NP-complete problem to it in polynomial time. Karp's 1972 paper did this for 21 problems, including clique, vertex cover, graph coloring and set cover, and Garey and Johnson's catalog lists hundreds more.

Common mistakes are reducing the new problem to SAT (that proves only membership), using a reduction whose output is exponentially large (it proves nothing), or reasoning from benchmark runtimes (they describe instances, not the problem). Independent set is NP-complete because clique reduces to it by complementing the graph, a polynomial step, and a candidate set checks quickly.

## NP-hard, NP-complete and the problems a tool meets

NP-hard means at least as hard as every NP problem, with no requirement to be in NP. Optimization versions such as "find the minimum-wirelength placement" are NP-hard when their decision versions are NP-complete. Some problems sit higher still: deciding whether a formula has an equivalent formula with at most $k$ literals is complete for the second level of the polynomial hierarchy, because a guessed small formula must also be verified equivalent on every input.

Special cases are often easy. Graph 2-coloring is bipartiteness, solved by breadth-first search, while 3-coloring is NP-complete; 2-SAT is linear while 3-SAT is NP-complete; exact two-level minimization is hard because its covering step is set cover and the number of primes can be exponential. Locating the hard core of a tool's problem tells you where heuristics must go and where an exact algorithm is affordable.

## Going deeper

label: From SAT to 3-SAT
lesson:
# From SAT to 3-SAT

3-SAT, where every clause has at most three literals, is the standard starting point for NP-hardness proofs because its instances are uniform and small gadgets can simulate a clause. It is NP-complete because general CNF-SAT reduces to it by splitting long clauses with fresh variables. The construction is also a lesson in equisatisfiable encodings: the new formula is not equivalent to the old one, but it is satisfiable exactly when the old one is, and that is all a reduction needs.

## Splitting one long clause

A clause $(l_1 \lor l_2 \lor \dots \lor l_k)$ with $k > 3$ is replaced by a chain linked by fresh variables $y_1, \dots, y_{k-3}$:
$$(l_1 \lor l_2 \lor y_1)(\neg y_1 \lor l_3 \lor y_2)(\neg y_2 \lor l_4 \lor y_3) \cdots (\neg y_{k-3} \lor l_{k-1} \lor l_k).$$
The first and last clauses take two original literals each and every middle clause one, so there are $k - 2$ clauses and $k - 3$ new variables. For $k = 5$: $(l_1 \lor l_2 \lor y_1)(\neg y_1 \lor l_3 \lor y_2)(\neg y_2 \lor l_4 \lor l_5)$, three clauses and two new variables.

If some $l_j$ is true, set $y_i = 1$ for the clauses before it and $y_i = 0$ after it, and every chain clause is satisfied. If every $l_j$ is false, the chain forces $y_1 = 1$, then $y_2 = 1$, and so on, until the last clause fails. So the chain is satisfiable exactly when the original clause is.

## Fresh variables for a whole formula

Each long clause gets its own fresh variables, so the total is $\sum_j (k_j - 3)$ over clauses with $k_j > 3$, and clauses with three or fewer literals add none. A CNF with clauses of sizes 9, 5, 8, 6 and 9 gains $6 + 2 + 5 + 3 + 6 = 22$ variables.

Clauses shorter than three can be padded with fresh variables if exact 3-literal clauses are required, or left alone for at-most-3-SAT. Either way the growth is linear in the size of the input, so the reduction is polynomial.

## Size of the 3-CNF

The new formula has $\sum_j (k_j - 2)$ clauses over the long clauses plus the short clauses unchanged. Sizes 7, 7 and 8 give $5 + 5 + 6 = 16$ clauses. The total number of literal occurrences grows by a factor of at most three, again linear.

The same chaining idea reappears in practice: the sequential-counter encoding of at-most-one constraints, the Tseitin encoding of wide gates and the splitting of long XORs all trade one big constraint for a linear number of small ones linked by auxiliary variables. Fewer literals per clause help unit propagation, but more variables can mean longer search, so solvers and encoders choose case by case.

## Going deeper

Garey and Johnson, "Computers and Intractability" (1979), section 3.1.1. Sipser, "Introduction to the Theory of Computation" (3rd ed., 2012), section 7.4.

label: Vertex cover, independent set and clique
lesson:
# Vertex cover, independent set and clique

Vertex cover, independent set and clique are three faces of one problem, and they appear throughout EDA: vertex cover in test-point selection and in breaking cycles, independent sets in conflict-free scheduling and in register binding, cliques in compatibility-based resource sharing. They are related by complementation, which turns any algorithm or hardness result for one into one for the others, and vertex cover is shown NP-hard by a classic gadget reduction from 3-SAT.

## Covers and independent sets are complements

A vertex cover is a set $C$ of vertices touching every edge. An independent set is a set $S$ with no edge inside it. A set $S$ is independent exactly when $V \setminus S$ is a vertex cover: an edge inside $S$ is precisely an edge the complement misses. So the maximum independent set has size $|V|$ minus the minimum vertex cover.

A graph with 26 vertices whose maximum independent set has 2 vertices has a minimum vertex cover of 24. The equivalence is exact for optimal solutions but not for approximations: a cover within a factor 2 of optimal gives an independent set with no comparable guarantee, which is why vertex cover is approximable and independent set is not.

## 3-SAT to vertex cover

The Garey-Johnson reduction builds, for a 3-CNF with $n$ variables and $m$ clauses, one edge per variable between vertices $x_i$ and $\neg x_i$, one triangle per clause, and an edge from each triangle corner to the literal vertex it represents. The graph has $2n + 3m$ vertices and $n + 6m$ edges (one per variable, three triangle edges and three links per clause), and the target is $k = n + 2m$.

Any cover needs at least one endpoint per variable edge and at least two corners per triangle, so $n + 2m$ is the minimum possible. A cover of exactly that size picks one literal per variable (an assignment) and leaves one corner per triangle uncovered by the triangle itself; that corner's link must be covered by its literal vertex, so the literal is true. For $n = 2$ and $m = 1$: 7 vertices, 8 edges, $k = 4$.

## Clique through the complement graph

A clique in $G$ is an independent set in the complement graph $\overline{G}$, which has the same vertices and exactly the edges $G$ lacks: $\binom{|V|}{2} - |E|$ of them. A graph with 5 vertices and 4 edges has a complement with $10 - 4 = 6$ edges. Building the complement takes polynomial time, so clique and independent set are polynomially equivalent, and both are NP-complete.

Complementation can blow up a sparse graph into a dense one, which matters in practice even though it is polynomial: a netlist conflict graph with $10^6$ vertices and a few million edges has a complement with about $5 \times 10^{11}$ edges. Tools therefore choose the formulation whose graph is sparse, and solve maximum independent set on the conflict graph rather than maximum clique on the compatibility graph, or vice versa.

## Going deeper

Garey and Johnson, "Computers and Intractability" (1979), section 3.1.3. Karp, "Reducibility among combinatorial problems" (1972).

prereqs: Vertex cover, independent set and clique
lesson:
# Approximation algorithms and heuristics

When a problem is NP-hard, a tool still has to return an answer quickly. An approximation algorithm runs in polynomial time and comes with a proven ratio: its cost is never worse than $\rho$ times the optimum. A heuristic runs fast and often does well but carries no such guarantee. EDA uses both: approximation ideas inside test compaction, covering and partitioning, and heuristics such as simulated annealing, local search and greedy rewriting almost everywhere. Knowing what a ratio promises, and what a heuristic does not, is basic engineering judgment.

## The matching-based vertex cover

Scan the edges in order; whenever an edge has neither endpoint in the cover, add both endpoints. The chosen edges form a maximal matching $M$, and the result is a cover of size $2|M|$. On the path with edges (1,2), (2,3), (3,4), the scan takes (1,2), skips (2,3), takes (3,4), and returns 4 vertices.

The proof of the ratio is two lines. The returned set covers every edge, or the scan would have taken that edge. Any cover, including the optimal one, needs a distinct vertex for each matched edge, since the matched edges share no endpoints, so $OPT \ge |M|$ and the algorithm's cost $2|M| \le 2 \cdot OPT$.

## What a ratio guarantees

A ratio is a worst-case bound over all instances, not a prediction for a given one. On the path above the optimum is $\{2, 3\}$, so the ratio achieved is $4/2 = 2$, the bound is tight. On other graphs the same algorithm may happen to be optimal. The matching also certifies a lower bound: $OPT \ge |M|$, so the algorithm can report how far from optimal it might be on this instance.

No polynomial algorithm with a ratio better than 2 is known for vertex cover. For independent set, by contrast, no polynomial algorithm achieves ratio $n^{1-\varepsilon}$ unless P = NP, so its exact complement relationship to vertex cover does not carry approximation over.

## Greedy set cover and heuristics without guarantees

Greedy set cover repeatedly picks the set covering the most uncovered elements. If the largest set has $d$ elements, greedy uses at most $H(d) \cdot OPT$ sets, where $H(d) = 1 + 1/2 + \dots + 1/d \le 1 + \ln d$. For $d = 8$, $H(8) \approx 2.718$: if the optimum is 4 tests, greedy returns at most $\lfloor 4 \times 2.718 \rfloor = 10$. Unless P = NP no polynomial algorithm does better than about $\ln n$ (Dinur and Steurer, 2014), so greedy is essentially the best possible.

Heuristics make no such promise. Simulated annealing for placement, Espresso's expand-irredundant-reduce loop and AIG rewriting scripts often beat any guaranteed algorithm on real designs, but their quality is measured on benchmarks, not proven. A disciplined tool reports the lower bound it knows (a matching, an LP relaxation) next to the heuristic's answer, so the gap is visible.

## Going deeper

label: Parameterized complexity
lesson:
# Parameterized complexity

Parameterized complexity measures running time in two quantities: the input size $n$ and a parameter $k$ such as the solution size or the treewidth. A problem is fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) when it can be solved in time $f(k) \cdot n^{O(1)}$, exponential only in the parameter. Many NP-hard EDA problems have small natural parameters, few faults to explain, few cuts, small treewidth of a netlist, so an FPT algorithm can be exact and fast on the instances that matter. Vertex cover parameterized by cover size is the canonical example.

## Bounded search trees

To decide whether a graph has a vertex cover of size at most $k$, pick any uncovered edge $(u, v)$. Some endpoint must be in the cover, so branch: take $u$ or take $v$, each lowering the budget by 1. The search tree has depth at most $k$ and at most $2^k$ leaves, with polynomial work per node, so the running time is $O(2^k n)$: for $k = 20$ that is about a million leaves, regardless of whether $n$ is a thousand or a million.

Smarter branching lowers the base. Branching on a vertex $v$ of degree at least 3, either take $v$ or take all of its neighbours, gives leaf counts $L(k) = L(k-1) + L(k-3)$, which grows like $1.4656^k$; the best known algorithms reach about $1.2738^k$. By contrast, clique parameterized by $k$ is W[1]-complete and believed not to be FPT, so the parameter alone does not make a problem easy.

## Kernelization: forced vertices

A kernel is a polynomial-time reduction to an equivalent instance whose size depends only on $k$. Buss's rule for vertex cover: a vertex of degree greater than $k$ must be in any cover of size at most $k$, because otherwise all of its more than $k$ neighbours would be. So take it, delete its edges, and lower the budget to $k - 1$. Repeat with the new budget until no vertex qualifies.

On a star with center 1 and 8 leaves plus one extra edge (3,4), with $k = 2$, vertex 1 has degree 8 > 2 and is forced. The budget drops to 1, and the remaining edge (3,4) has endpoints of degree 1, so the rule stops after forcing one vertex.

## The kernel size bound

After the rule stops with budget $k'$, every vertex has degree at most $k'$, so $k'$ vertices can cover at most $k'^2$ edges. If more than $k'^2$ edges remain, the answer is no immediately; otherwise the remaining graph has at most $k'^2$ edges and is solved by the search tree.

In the example $k' = 1$ and one edge remains, within the bound $1^2 = 1$, and taking vertex 3 finishes the cover $\{1, 3\}$. Kernelization is preprocessing with a guarantee, the theoretical version of what SAT preprocessors and logic-synthesis sweeps do in practice: shrink the instance by rules that are always safe before spending exponential effort.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# SAT and BDD engines as agent tools

In an agent-first flow, SAT solvers, BDD packages and simulators are not libraries buried inside one program; they are skills an agent calls through a typed tool interface, the way engines are exposed over MCP. The agent decides what to ask, the compiled engine does the search. For that to be safe, the interface must say exactly what goes in, what can come out, under what limits, and how much each kind of answer can be trusted. A Boolean engine with a sloppy interface turns timeouts into false proofs.

## Typed inputs and outputs

The input should be a well-defined format: CNF in DIMACS form, an AIG in AIGER form, or a netlist the tool converts itself. Accepting an AIG is better than demanding CNF, because the engine keeps the structure (gates, fanout, levels) it needs for simulation, structural hashing and choosing cut points. Every call also carries its resource limits (time, conflicts, memory) and its random seed, so a run, and especially an inconclusive run, can be reproduced.

The output has three cases, not two: SAT with a model, UNSAT with an optional proof, or UNKNOWN with the limit that was hit. A BDD tool's output must include the variable order, since node counts are meaningless without it. Collapsing UNKNOWN into UNSAT, or returning a bare boolean, is the most dangerous interface bug a Boolean tool can have.

## What the manifest advertises

The agent selects an engine from its manifest, a short description of what it does, what it is good at, its limits and failure modes, and its tunable parameters. Selection is a cheap text decision; the expensive search stays in the compiled engine. The design data is not in the manifest.

Manifests encode real knowledge. A BDD skill should warn that some functions blow up under every variable order; Bryant proved this for the middle bits of multipliers, so an agent asked to compare two 32 by 32 multipliers should pick a SAT- or hashing-based equivalence engine. Two SAT configurations tuned for structured industrial instances and for uniform random 3-SAT should say so, because miters of synthesized netlists are structured instances where learning and restarts pay off.

## Trusting the answer

Answers differ in how they are checked. A SAT model is its own certificate: the agent evaluates every clause under it, in linear time, before using it. An UNSAT answer has no short certificate in general, so signoff-grade flows ask the solver for a DRAT proof and validate it with an independent checker. UNKNOWN carries no information at all; it must never be recorded as equivalence or as a bug.

When a large equivalence check times out, the sound responses are to decompose the problem (sweep internal equivalences, introduce cut points, prove smaller miters) or to raise the budget, while the transform stays unapproved. Approving because no counterexample was found, or rejecting because no proof was found, both confuse the absence of an answer with an answer.

## Going deeper

label: Fast and exact Boolean reasoning modes
prereqs: Fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop
lesson:
# Fast and exact Boolean reasoning modes

Every Boolean engine has a fast mode and an exact mode. Random or guided simulation, structural hashing and cheap signatures run in microseconds and can only refute; SAT, BDDs and proof-producing checkers are complete but can take arbitrarily long. An agent running a continuous optimization loop must use the fast mode for almost everything and the exact mode exactly where a decision is committed. Getting the boundary wrong either wastes compute or ships a wrong circuit.

## Simulation as the fast mode

Simulating $t$ random vectors through an original circuit and a proposed rewrite costs a few word operations per gate per 64 vectors. A mismatch is a definite counterexample. A clean run is weak evidence: if the rewrite were wrong on $d$ of $2^n$ inputs, it would escape with probability $(1 - d/2^n)^t$.

For a 12-input block, a rewrite wrong on 2 inputs, and 4,096 vectors, the escape probability is $(1 - 2/4096)^{4096} \approx e^{-2} \approx 0.135$. One such bug in seven survives the run. For a 64-input block no simulation budget gets near certainty. So the fast mode can rank and filter candidates, but its "probably equal" is a hypothesis, not a verdict.

## Exact engines as the accurate mode

SAT on the miter, or a BDD comparison where BDDs stay small, decides equivalence on every input. SAT-sweeping engines combine the modes: simulation splits nodes into candidate equivalence classes, SAT is called only on pairs that survive, and every counterexample SAT finds is added to the simulation vectors, where it often splits many other classes at once.

Only an exact engine can produce the verdict "equal on every input". It is also the expensive step, so a well-built loop budgets it: limit conflicts per call, try the cheapest candidates first, and treat UNKNOWN as unresolved rather than as either answer.

## When the agent must recurse

The rule is simple: escalate to the exact engine before any transform is committed to the design or reported as equivalent. Ranking 200 candidate rewrites by estimated savings needs no proof, because a wrong rank costs only a little optimization; the 5 rewrites actually kept must each pass an exact check. A mismatch found by simulation needs no escalation at all, because it is already a definite answer.

Log the mode that produced each verdict. A downstream step that sees "equivalent (simulation, 4,096 vectors)" can demand a proof; one that sees an unlabeled "equivalent" cannot. Provenance is what keeps the fast loop honest when many agents and tools share one design database.

## Going deeper

Mishchenko, Chatterjee, Jiang and Brayton, "FRAIGs: a unifying representation for logic synthesis and verification", UC Berkeley technical report (2005). Kuehlmann, Paruthi, Krohm and Ganai, "Robust Boolean reasoning for equivalence checking and functional property verification", IEEE TCAD (2002).

label: Equivalence checking as the golden test
lesson:
# Equivalence checking as the golden test

When an agent proposes a logic transform, a rewrite, a resynthesized cone, a remapped block, the golden test is a combinational equivalence check between the original and the proposal. It is the Boolean domain's version of a golden regression: deterministic, complete, and cheap enough to run on every proposed change. A transform that has not passed it is not a transform, only a suggestion. Building the check correctly, including what it assumes about don't cares, is what makes an agentic optimization loop safe.

## The miter

The miter joins the two circuits on shared primary inputs, XORs their outputs, and asks a SAT solver whether the XOR can be 1. Any model is a counterexample input; UNSAT means the circuits agree on every input. With several outputs, XOR them pairwise and OR the results.

Suppose $f = d + \overline{a}\,\overline{d} + b\overline{c}d + \overline{b}c$ is rewritten as $g = d + \overline{a}\,\overline{d} + bd + \overline{b}c$. Both reduce to $d + \overline{a} + \overline{b}c$, since $b\overline{c}d$ and $bd$ are both absorbed by $d$, so the miter has no model and the rewrite is accepted. If instead $g$ dropped the term $\overline{a}\,\overline{d}$, the miter would be satisfied by the inputs with $a = 0$, $d = 0$ and not ($b = 0$, $c = 1$), and the solver would return one of them.

## The size of the check

With the Tseitin encoding the miter's CNF is linear in the two circuits: each $k$-input AND, OR, NAND or NOR adds $k + 1$ clauses, each two-input XOR or XNOR adds 4, each inverter 2, then 4 for the miter XOR and 1 for the unit clause asserting it. An original block with one two-input XOR, one three-input AND, one two-input OR and an inverter (13 clauses), compared with a rewrite of 14 clauses, gives a miter of $13 + 14 + 4 + 1 = 32$ clauses.

Linear size is what makes the golden test affordable on every transform in a loop. Runtime is a different matter, since UNSAT miters of restructured logic can be hard; practical checkers first hash both circuits together so identical structure merges, then sweep internal equivalences so the final miter is small.

## Equivalence up to don't cares

Transforms often exploit don't cares: inputs that cannot occur, or outputs nobody observes. Then the right check is equivalence on the care set: the miter is conjoined with a constraint excluding the don't-care inputs, and only mismatches on care inputs count. If $f$ and $g$ differ on five inputs and three of them are certified unreachable, two real counterexamples remain and the transform is rejected.

The don't-care set is part of the claim and must come from a trusted analysis, such as reachability or a verified environment constraint, never from the agent that proposed the transform. A check that accepts any don't-care set the agent supplies can be passed by declaring every mismatch a don't care.

## Going deeper

Kuehlmann and Krohm, "Equivalence checking using cuts and heaps", DAC (1997). Mishchenko, Chatterjee, Brayton and Een, "Improvements to combinational equivalence checking", ICCAD (2006).

label: Change tiers in a Boolean reasoning engine
lesson:
# Change tiers in a Boolean reasoning engine

When an agent or a user asks for a change in a SAT solver or BDD package, the first decision is where the change belongs. The four-layer model, immutable core, policy, parameters and observation hooks, says what can be changed cheaply and what needs human approval and full regression. Boolean engines are an ideal case study because their cores are small and correctness-critical (a wrong UNSAT is a false proof) while their behavior is dominated by tunable heuristics.

## Core, policy, parameters and hooks

In a CDCL solver the core is clause semantics, unit propagation, conflict analysis correctness and proof logging: anything whose bug produces a wrong answer. Policy is the decision heuristic, the restart strategy and the clause-deletion scheme. Parameters are activity decay factors, restart intervals and conflict limits. Hooks report conflict counts, learned-clause statistics and trail depth to whoever is watching.

In a BDD package the core is the unique table and the canonicity invariants: no duplicate nodes, no node whose children are equal. Variable reordering methods, sifting or window permutation, are policy; node limits, cache sizes and reordering thresholds are parameters; a callback on garbage collection is a hook.

## Landing a request in a tier

Try the smallest tier first. "Restart more often on our bounded model checking jobs" is Tier 1, a parameter change with no recompile. "Use a variable order that interleaves the bits of the two operand buses", when the package offers only static and sifting orders, is Tier 2, a new policy at an existing seam. "Store clauses differently to support a new proof format" touches clause storage and proof logging, the core, so it is Tier 3: a human-approved diff and the full regression suite.

Passing golden tests is necessary, not sufficient. A plug-in heuristic that gives correct answers but runs 40% slower must also be compared against the baseline on the benchmark suite before it is promoted. Correctness is checked by golden tests; quality is decided by differential QoR and runtime.

## Seams for Boolean engines

A seam is a narrow interface the core calls at a well-defined point. A decision-heuristic seam in a SAT solver exposes read-only search state, variable activities, the assignment trail and the decision level, and returns a literal; it never gets write access to the clause database, which would let a plug-in break soundness. A variable-order seam in a BDD package accepts and returns a permutation, while the core rebuilds the diagram and keeps it canonical.

Seams must be coarse and deterministic. Propagation is the hot loop, executed millions of times per second, so a plug-in call there would block inlining and dominate runtime; calls belong at decisions, restarts or reorderings. A plug-in that seeds a random generator from the clock breaks reproducibility, and with it every golden and differential test.

## Going deeper

Een and Sorensson, "An extensible SAT-solver", SAT (2003), on MiniSat's design. Somenzi, CUDD: CU Decision Diagram Package documentation, on reordering and the unique table.

# Tool-grounded rewards for logic transforms

Training a model to propose logic rewrites with reinforcement learning needs a reward, and the natural reward comes from tools: an equivalence checker says whether the rewrite is correct, structural hashing and a node count say whether it helps. Because the tools are deterministic and exact, the reward is grounded in ground truth rather than in another model's opinion. The risks are equally concrete: a reward computed with a weak check or a sloppy metric will be gamed, and a proxy metric can drift from the quality that signoff measures.

## Scoring a proposed transform

A sound reward gates on correctness and then measures gain: $R = [\text{miter UNSAT}] \times (N_{before} - N_{after}) / N_{before}$, where $N$ is the AND-node count after structural hashing. A rewrite from 1,200 to 1,050 nodes that is proven equivalent earns $150 / 1200 = 0.125$; dividing by the new size instead (0.143) is a common slip. A rewrite that fails the check earns nothing, however small it is.

Both counts must come from the same pipeline, hashed the same way, or the reward measures representation noise. If the design is timing-critical the reward also needs a depth or delay term, since a rewrite that saves nodes by adding logic levels can make the block worse.

## How a reward gets gamed

A policy maximizes whatever the reward actually checks. If equivalence is tested with 1,000 random vectors instead of SAT, the policy learns rewrites that are wrong on rare inputs. If a SAT timeout is scored as "no counterexample found", it learns rewrites that make the miter hard, so checks time out and pay out. If the reward accepts don't cares without verifying them, it learns to change behavior on reachable inputs and call them don't care.

Metric mismatches are gamed too: if the baseline is counted on an unhashed netlist and the result on a hashed one, the policy is credited for hashing it did not do. The defense is the same each time: make the reward use the exact check, the trusted care set and one consistent measurement pipeline, and score UNKNOWN as zero or a penalty.

## From proxy to signoff

AIG node count is a fast proxy. After technology mapping, area and delay are what count, and the two can diverge: an 8% node reduction may yield 1% mapped area. Periodically validating rewards against mapped QoR, and reweighting when they drift, keeps the proxy honest; this gap between proxy reward and signoff QoR is the central risk of tool-grounded RL.

Some parts never leave the loop. The exact equivalence check runs on every accepted rewrite, however good the policy becomes, because correctness cannot be learned to a guarantee. Rewards are computed with fixed solver versions, seeds and limits, so identical outputs earn identical rewards and training runs are reproducible.

## Going deeper
